title: Johnny English
full_review:
A bumbling British secret agent must recover the stolen crown jewels and prevent a loony Frenchman from usurping the throne of England in the silly spy comedy "Johnny English" (Universal).

Staring Rowan Atkinson and directed by Peter Howitt, the film is the cinematic equivalent of English cuisine: bland and unappetizing. It's full of crude toilet humor and doltish sight gags.

The, ahem, plot revolves around Johnny English, a junior agent in MI-5, the British Secret Service. Lacking the Bond-like looks, skills and savoir fare of uber-operative Agent One, English is a legend in his own mind, pushing papers for queen and country while entertaining Walter Mitty daydreams of romance and international intrigue. But when Agent One is killed in action and the remaining roster of field agents is erased in an explosion at his funeral service, English is called into action.

His first assignment is a security detail at the unveiling of the newly restored crown jewels. The treasure is filched from right under the nose of the bungling Brit buffoon by a megalomaniac Frenchy named Pascal Sauvage (John Malkovich), who plans to use the royal rocks as part of a hokey plot to steal the English crown. After the bogus coronation the Gaul has the gall to suggest converting the entire scepter'd isle into a massive penal colony, leaving it up to English and Lorna Campbell (Natalie Imbruglia), his sexy Interpol sidekick, to stop Sauvage's foie-gras madness.

Of course the sketchy story line merely serves the perfunctory role of connecting the ensuing cloak-and-dagger silliness which Atkinson plays with comedic acumen. Echoing shades of Monty Python mirth, his patented blend of wry aloofness and physical zaniness provides some genuinely funny moments and should please fans of the rubber-faced funnyman best known for his work on the "Mr. Bean" and "Black Adder" BBC TV series.

That being said, much of "Johnny English" feels like a retread, playing many of the same joke cards as the "Austin Powers" films -- without the bad teeth and shagadelic wardrobe. However, while both Brit spy spoof franchises rely heavily on crude bathroom farce, Atkinson's parody downplays the sexual humor, jettisoning the wink-wink innuendo of Mike Myers' libidinous psychedelic man of mystery.

It should be noted that there are two scenes which push the envelope of good taste. One contains a disgusting sight gag involving defecation and another mocking the archbishop of Canterbury, the highest cleric in the Church of England, who is forced to drop his drawers during a pomp-filled ceremony in order to disprove accusations of a blasphemous tattoo on his buttocks.

Aside from such base episodes, a lot of the film's more subtle wit is fueled by an inherent English Francophobic bias which -- like much of British humor -- may not resonate with American audiences, current American-French relations notwithstanding. In one of the movie's few clever barbs, a British radio station is hosting an on-air celebration for Sauvage's coronation. The DJ announces that there is still time to call with the top hundred things to like about the French -- noting after a short pause, "We haven't had any calls yet." Earlier, English quips, "The only thing the French should be allowed to host is an invasion."

Atkinson originated the Johnny English character for a series of British TV commercials for Barclay Bank, which may prove hilarious for a 30-second spot but when stretched over 90 minutes grows quickly stale.

This comic take on British intelligence, while wholly British, is only at times intelligent.

Due to crude toilet and sexual humor, a blasphemous sight gag, comic rear nudity and some mild profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
